articleTitle: Electrode charge injection: Lessons from electrochemistry
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Localized electronic charges in disordered solids can be described in terms of ions. The transfer of charge to and from electrodes corresponds then, to the oxidation/ reduction of molecular species. The study of these charge injecting redox processes forms a fundamental and growing segment of electrochemical research. The theoretical bases for these studies are deceptively concise and are briefly reviewed. The experimental predictions resulting from these foundations focus on the current-voltage relationships and on the frequency/time dependence of the interfacial impedance. The bulk of the substantiating evidence comes from the redox of active species in solution. New theoretical and experimental results relating to active species which are rigidly anchored to the electrode are presented. These results are compared to unpublished data on the electrode/organic photoconductor interface.

articleTitle: Static charge accumulated by epoxy post insulation stressed at high DC voltages
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Solid insulators are used for support in many types of high voltage apparatus. Because these supports are often composed of high resistivity materials, static charges may be accumulated and held by them for extended periods of time. The electric field distribution in the vicinity of the insulator is then altered so that electrical breakdown in the surrounding gas may result.

articleTitle: Water tree propagation in relation to mechanical properties of polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: A large number of papers have already been devoted to investigations of water treeing in polyethylene insulation and many experimental data are available. A variety of mechanisms have been proposed but none of them is entirely satisfactory. In this paper, we do not present any new experimental observations. Our work is restricted to considerations of the influence of the mechanical properties of polyethylene on the propagation of the trees.

articleTitle: Effects of gas phase on tree initiation in polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: A simple model was proposed by two of the authors for tree initiation in polyethylene,<sup>1</sup>»<sup>2</sup> in which the repeated process of charge injection and extraction between the electrode and the dielectric is responsible for tree initiation. It is made either directly between the two or indirectly via a certain gas phase which is considered to exist inevitably between the two. The former process is related to an electronic barrier which electrons are forced to jump over or tunnel through, i.e., the work function of a metal minus electron affinity of a dielectric. This paper deals with the latter process. Two kinds of experiments were carried out. First, a hypodermic needle was inserted into a polyethylene slab so that any kind of gas might be introduced to the tip of the needle. The test specimen referred to as the treeing specimen in this paper was set in a stainless steel cell filled with slightly pressurized SF<inf>6</inf>. Gases such as air, N<inf>2</inf>, O<inf>2</inf> and SF<inf>6</inf> were introduced from an outer gas reservoir to the needle system. Tree initiation voltages, corona pulse height spectra and shapes of the generated trees in their early stage were investigated. Second, a sewing-needle was used facing a polyethylene slab grounded on its opposite side. This is called the free space specimen in the paper for convenience. Corona starting voltages and pulse height distribution characteristics were measured when the stainless steel cell was filled with either air, N<inf>2</inf>, O<inf>2</inf> or SF<inf>6</inf> at atmospheric pressure. It is concluded that the existence of a thin gas-layer between a metal electrode and a dielectric will affect the tree initiation voltage in a typical treeing experiment, but that it is not caused by any preceding gaseous discharge. A process may be involved that the work function of a dielectric at its surface is affected by a gas through adsorption or chemical reaction, resulting in the change in the probability of electron injection.

articleTitle: Measurement of prebreakdown electric fields in liquid insulants
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: In recent years, optical techniques have been used to identify and classify prebreakdown phenomena in liquid insulating materials.<sup>1–8</sup> This report describes an attempt to duplicate selected previous results and to extent them by combining time-resolved shadowgraphs with time-resolved electric field measurements using the electro-optic Kerr effect. The addition of electric field measurement permits a determination of the effect of space charge on breakdown and provides information as to whether or not prebreakdown trees are electrical conductors.

articleTitle: Effect of microvoids on V-t characteristics and tree growth in crosslinked polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Crosslinked polyethylene is being used as an insulation of electric power cables because of its excellent quality. But in spite of the fact that polyethylene and corsslinked polyethylene cables have established an excellent service record, it was reported that some polyethylene and crosslinked polyethylene cables had failed in service over several years.<sup>1,2</sup> This might be because the quality of polyethylene or crosslinked polyethylene is deteriorated by trees initiated and grown at an asymmetrical conductor or a void under a high electric field. In fact, careful microscopic analysis of polyethylene or crosslinked polyethylene cable which had been in service for several years had found various types of trees.<sup>1, 2</sup>

articleTitle: Charge storage and transport in polymers
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: A number of recent studies have been devoted to problems concerning storage and transport of electronic charges in polymers. Of particular interest are questions relating to the transport of charge carriers in thin films of highly insulating polymers. In general, charge transport is studied by measurements of external integral parameters such as the decay of the surface potential. These quantities are, in experimental situations, related to internal parameters in a nonunique manner. Thus the conclusions that can be drawn about internal phenomena are very limited. It is therefore important to supplement measurements of external parameters by data about internal quantities, such as the charge or potential distribution.

articleTitle: The partial discharge and breakdown characteristics of insulating tapes immersed in liquid nitrogen
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Electrical power apparatus operating at cryogenic temperatures offers advantages over conventional equipment and research is continuing to produce superconducting generators and cables in addition to cryoresistive cables. Although there have been a limited number of studies of the behaviour of electrical insulation for such equipment,<sup>1,2</sup> the operating stresses have not been evaluated and little is known of the ageing mechanisms. This paper describes the initial results of a project to determine suitable operating stresses and to study the deterioration of polymeric tapes immersed in a cryogenic fluid while subjected to high electric stresses. Partial discharge and breakdown characteristics of fibrous insulating sheets with and without artificial cavities are reported.

articleTitle: Breakdown between dielectric coated electrodes in compressed gases with metallic particle contamination
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Metallic particle contamination can play a crucial role in compressed gas insulated apparatus. The application of a dielectric coating to an electrode surface should hamper the charging of a metallic particle and hence increase the lift off field at which particle motion commences. The effect of dielectric coatings (polyurethane, epoxy and anodized oxide layers) on the particle lift off field has been previously reported.<sup>1</sup> The authors have extensively explored the effect of anodized oxide coatings on lifting field and breakdown between plane parallel aluminum electrodes in compressed sulphur hexafluoride gas. Some experiments have also been performed in nitrogen. In general anodized oxide coatings produce the following results under 60 Hz voltages: (a) The lifting field for the various metallic particles is increased by a factor of two or more if the lower electrode is anodized. (b) The coating thickness, the size, shape and material of the particle do not appear to have a significant influence on the lifting field. (c) The lifting field increases with gas pressure and this increase is more noticeable with thicker (> 100 μ) anodized oxide layers. (d) The lifting field in sulphur hexafluoride gas is higher than in nitrogen.

articleTitle: Wetting and tracking breakdown of organic insulating materials in an atmosphere of mist
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Tracking breakdown under wetting condition has been studied recently due to the large number of organic insulating materials used for outdoor service. In this paper, the wetting and the deterioration process for tracking breakdown of organic insulating materials in an atmosphere of fine mist formed by ultra-sonic vibration is investigated with attention to contact angle of droplets, discharge inception time, carbonization inception time, progress time of carbonization and tracking breakdown time.

articleTitle: Charge storage and transport in solid dielectrics (The case of irradiated polymers)
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: “The subject (of the anomalous properties of dielectrics) is somewhat special and one which until quite recently has not attracted the interest which it deserves from electrical engineers. There is an important relation between the anomalous properties of dielectrics and the performance of high voltage insulation. The literature on the subject reveals an enormous quantity of experimental results and attempts at theoretical analysis. There is, however, the widest divergence of point of view and almost complete absence of a common ground. As a consequence it seemed to me worthwhile to attempt some coordination and to bring together in some form the more important results of all this work.”

articleTitle: Post-irradiation thermally stimulated currents in organic insulators
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Thermally stimulated conductivity (TSC) in insulating materials following their exposure to ionizing radiation has been studied by various workers, using a variety of methods of irradiation; these include electrons, corona discharge, X- and γ-rays.

articleTitle: Electrical current decay in polyethylene after irradiation with monoenergetic electron beam
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Decay of induced current in low density polyethylene (density, 0.920 g/cc) was investigated after irradiation with a partially penetrating monoenergetic electron beam of 0.8 MeV. The values of the mobility of free electron under irradiation were estimated using the analysis of Gross et al.<sup>1</sup> The relation between charges injected into polyethylene and the values of the decay current was also investigated.

articleTitle: Describing relaxing systems which evolve with time
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: An apparent distribution of relaxation times, or “non-Debye” behaviour, seems closer to being the rule than the exception in dielectric and mechanical relaxation,<sup>1,2</sup> and a material maintained at constant temperature will behave as if it had such a distribution of relaxation times whether (a) it has a constant distribution of constant relaxation times (b) it has a constant distribution of evolving relaxation times, even if only a single time constant which alters with the passage of time (and which in this case is then the reciprocal of the “time-dependent hazard” h(t) mentioned later) (c) it has an evolving distribution of constant relaxation times, or (d) it has an evolving distribution of evolving relaxation times.

articleTitle: Low temperature dielectric loss characteristics of polypropylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: The dielectric loss of several commercial polypropylene films having different morphologies has been measured at temperatures in the range 4.2–273K. The effect of annealing on the dielectric loss characteristics of the film has also been examined. Significant differences in loss behavior were observed between unannealed films as well as between unannealed and annealed films. Loss peaks were variously observed at 130K (γ peak) and 30K. Evidence pointing to an apparent loss peak below 4.2K has also been obtained. The 30K peak corresponds to one previously found in mechanical relaxation experiments. The apparent existence of a peak below 4.2K may, by analogy with studies on polyethylene, be attributed to the presence of antioxidant. The suitability of polypropylene, in tape form, as electric insulation for superconducting high power transmission cables operated at 6–9K, will be discussed in the light of the present study.

articleTitle: Poling of poly(vinylidene fluoride) at high electric fields
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Bernhard Gross and electrets soon become associative terms to anyone entering the fields of electrets. A list of his more than 130 publications can be found in the front of a book resulting from the International Symposium on Electrets and Dielectrics<sup>1</sup> held in Sao Carlos, Brazil in honour of his 70th birthday. It contains at least 32 papers related to electrets. I am pleased to contribute to a technical session following Professor Gross's J. B. Whitehead Memorial Lecture.

articleTitle: Thermal aging effects in corona charged polyvinylidene fluoride
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVF2) is a semicrystalline polymer which may exist in at least two stable forms<sup>1</sup> simultaneously, ie‥, a planar zig-zag polar form (Form 1 or 3-form) with two monomer units -CF<inf>2</inf>-CH<inf>2</inf>-per unit cell belonging to the space group Cm2m(C<sup>14</sup><inf>2V</inf>) and the non-polar T-G-T-G' form (Form 2 or α-form) with the space group P2<inf>1</inf>/C(C<inf>2h</inf><sup>5</sup>). In the Form 1 structure each monomer unit of PVF<inf>2</inf> has a dipole moment of 2.1D (≡7.01 × 10<sup>−30</sup> Coulomb-metre) which is oriented perpendicular to the polymer chain axis. It has been suggested<sup>2</sup> that in PVF<inf>2</inf> films, containing both Form 1 and Form 2 crystallites, the piezo- and pyro-electric responses may increase with increasing Form 1 content. It is also established that the piezo- and pyroelectric responses in oriented PVF2 films are enhanced on poling (i.e. subjecting the polymer to a high electrical stress at an elevated temperature for an extended period of time). Oshiki and Fukada<sup>3</sup> observe a conversion from Form 2 to Form 1 on stretching and subsequent poling of PVF<inf>2</inf> films. It has also been shown<sup>4</sup> that a change in molecular structure may occur in bi-axially oriented PVF<inf>2</inf> films subsequent to poling by corona charging. These facts tend to suggest that a dipolar orientation in the crystalline and (or) amorphous phase may occur in PVF<inf>2</inf> on poling. The relevance of the changes in the crystalline structure on poling and the nature of the stability of the PVF<inf>2</inf> thermo-electrets on subsequent thermal cycling are not yet understood.

articleTitle: Effects of additives on breakdown in polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: In 1975 we reported<sup>1,2</sup> on a new approach to tree inhibition in dielectrics making use of field grading at asperities based on a field-dependent conductivity. Initially we attempted to take advantage of the second Wien effect, i.e., field enhanced dissociation of ionic additives. While such additives were only marginally successful we found a number of non-ionic materials which markedly increased the tree inception and breakdown voltage.<sup>3</sup> During this period several other non-ionic tree inhibitors were reported.<sup>4–6</sup> One explanation for the effectiveness of these additives might be that they increase the intrinic strength of polyethylene. In this paper we examine this hypothesis.

articleTitle: A model for combined environment accelerated aging applied to a neoprene cable jacketing material
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: The present paper describes some results of a continuing program at Sandia Laboratories whose main goal is to develop more reliable accelerated aging techniques. An interesting situation in accelerated aging occurs when two or more environmental stresses lead to the deterioration of a component. Synergism is sometimes important in such cases so that the deteriorating effects of the various environments are not additive. We have proposed a model<sup>1</sup> potentially applicable to combined environment aging. This paper will outline the model and indicate how it can be used to carry out accelerated aging in combined environment situations. Some preliminary data on a neoprene cable jacketing material aged in single and combined thermal and radiation environments will be described and analyzed according to the formalism of the model.

articleTitle: Dielectric strength of crosslinked polyethylene insulation part II effect of impregnation and in situ polymerization
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Crosslinked polyethylene, an ideal insulation for high voltage transmission and distribution cables, often contains a large number (≈10<sup>6</sup> per cm<sup>2</sup>) of microvoids.<sup>1</sup> The electric stress intensification occurring at these voids can lead to electrical<sup>2</sup> and electrochemical treeing.<sup>3</sup> We reported in an earlier communcaiton<sup>4</sup> that impregnation of slabs cut from a 138 kV cable with mineral oil and polyethylene wax increases the dielectric strength. These imprégnants are liquid at the peak service temperature (90°C) and hence they may exude during the service life of the cable. We propose that impregnating the cable with a monomer-catalyst solution and polymerizing the monomer insitu may heal the voids permanently. In this paper we will present the results of impregnation of crosslinked polyethylene slabs with two monomers (lauryl methacrylate and vinyl toluene) and their subsequent insitu polymerization through free radical initiation. The effect of impregnation on void filling and breakdown strength will be discussed.

articleTitle: Quantized relaxation of polarization
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Whitehead<sup>1</sup> reviewing early work quotes that Kohlraush as early as 1845 suggested the decay current formula i = a.t<sup>−n</sup> and surprisingly the physical reasons for this relationship still remain the subject of discussion. For electronic conductors, Walden<sup>2</sup> and Wintle<sup>3</sup> have provided extensive evidence that the discharge currents are mainly due to trapped space charge in the region around the electrodes. There are however many others who prefer the theory of Debye and its extension by Cole that for polar dielectrics the decay of current with time is caused by the relaxation of polarization mechanisms having a wide range of distributed activation energies. Jonscher<sup>4</sup> suggests that the discharge can be usually explained by a small number of processes of different and specific activation energies. Das Gupta and Joyner,<sup>5</sup> in a recent review which also included decay current measurements on polypropylene films, suggested that the relaxation of charge formed during the charging period is responsible for the effects observed at room temperature and that the contribution of the dipole relaxation is small. However Adamec and Calderwood<sup>6</sup> concluded from extensive studies of non-polar polymers that at room temperature and at low fields the depolarization current is due to the relaxation of polarization within the bulk of the dielectric.

articleTitle: Wound repair using foil electrets
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: It is known that in living tissue a current surrounding an injury arises as a result of the tissue damage. Such currents are the result of the disruption of the cellular membrane integrity which permits the chemical milieu to be altered as the ionic content of the cell spills out into the extracellular fluid.<sup>1</sup> It has been postulated that this bioelectric current contributes in some manner to the process of wound repair.

articleTitle: Spectroscopic study of the structural changes observed in doped polyethylene during its polarization process
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: In several kind of Polymers such as Polyethylene<sup>1–2</sup> or Poly(vinylidene fluoride),<sup>3</sup> we have observed, by Raman and infrared spectroscopy, rather important structural changes during the polarization process by a high electro­static field. This effect is a function of the intensity of the poling field and it is generally emphasized by a thermal treatment during the polarization.

articleTitle: Dielectric properties of alternating copolymers of maleic acid
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Presence of some divalent counterions in polyelectrolyte solutions enhances the low frequency dielectric increment of the solutions. The effect has been found in aqueous solutions of poly-(acrylic acid),<sup>1</sup> poly(methacrylic acid),<sup>2</sup> polyvinylamine,<sup>2</sup> and poly(styrene sulfonic acid),<sup>3</sup> when these polyions were neutralized with mixtures of mono- and divalent bases [such as NaOH and Ca(OH)<inf>2</inf> for polyacids].

articleTitle: Partial discharge performance of lapped plastic insulation for superconducting power transmission cables and the dielectric strength of supercritical helium gas
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) has been working on a project to develop a superconducting power transmission cable since 1972. A flexible ac cable with Nb<inf>3</inf>Sn superconductor force-cooled by supercritical helium, was the design selected.<sup>1</sup> Any dielectric used in a superconducting cable must have a very low dissipation factor so that the heat load to the refrigeration system is minimized. Differential contraction during cooling makes it impossible to use extruded dielectric, so a lapped, multilayer plastic tape construction was selected, with supercritical helium gas filling the butt spaces between tapes. Evaluation of many different tapes<sup>2</sup> has shown biaxially oriented laminated polypropylene tape to be a promising dielectric.

articleTitle: Study of the evolution of electrical treeing by observation of luminous phenomena and discharge detection
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Fewer articles dealing with discharge detection and light emission which accompanies the discharges than those concerning electrical treeing are published. Kosaki et al.<sup>1</sup> are interested in the detection of light emitted at the point of high voltage electrode when charges, injected into the material by field effects, recombine with holes of the lattice. It is therefore a study which aims at clarifying the physical processes involved in the initiation phase, since no treeing configuration is present in the solid when the emission occurs. Calderwood et al.<sup>2</sup> have studied low level (4/1000 pc) discharge detection during initiation phase.

articleTitle: Steep-front impulse breakdown of transformer insulation
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: For some years, a research project has been undertaken to investigate lightning damage of distribution transformers in Queensland. Previous work has resulted in a substantial reduction in the failure rate, and the current work is aimed at an investigation of the cause(s) of the remaining failures (about 0.3 percent per annum). Distribution transformers and their protecting lightning arresters are exposed to direct lightning strokes, and can therefore be subjected to over-voltages of severity considerably greater than occur in standard laboratory impulse tests. Standards call for tests with impulses of about 100 kV rising in 1 μs — the average rate of rise resulting from a direct strike is about 1500 kV/μs, with an upper limit of about 4000 kV/μs. In this paper, we report on the results of steep-front impulse voltage tests on typical distribution transformer insulation, including oil gaps, inter-twin and inter-layer insulation. Measurements of time-to-breakdown were made in the range 0.05 to 1 μsec, and the resulting volt-time curves are compared with similar measurements previously made on lightning arresters. The steep-front breakdown data are analysed using normal and extreme value statistics.

articleTitle: Some effects of particles on discharges in oil/paper systems
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: The influence of particles on partial discharges and voltage breakdown in oil has been summarized previously by the authors.<sup>1</sup> In this paper, the effect of particles on the breakdown of a more complex system of impregnated paper in series with an oil gap is discussed. Due to the long times involved for complete drying and impregnation, the number of test specimens employed was limited as was the number of complete voltage breakdowns. On the other hand, for paper in series with oil, partial discharges often occurred and these could be measured before breakdown took place. Under direct voltage, the leakage current and the desorption current were also measured. For the work described here, 2–5 μm iron particles were added to the oil. Particle motion was observed and photographed.

articleTitle: Phenomena in biological dielectrics
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: This paper is intended to provide an introduction to this session which is co-sponsored by the Dielectrics Society. It will consider experimental difficulties encountered in working with biomedical materials, the techniques available to reduce these difficulties and the kind of results which are obtained. An invited paper will then deal with non-linear dielectric properties which occur when very large polarizable molecules are present in the dielectric material.

articleTitle: Electric moment autocorrelation function of a model biopolymer
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Computer simulations of molecular assemblies have been of much help during the last twenty years towards an understanding of the link between microscopic structure and macroscopic quantities, including in some cases the static and dynamic dielectric properties of polar molecules. The purpose of the present work is to obtain, by this same technique, information concerning the electric-moment autocorrelation-function for macromolecules exhibiting an internal transition of the helix-coil type. A rigorous study of that kind would require both the use of the so-called method of Molecular Dynamics and consideration of the detailed structure of a given biopolymer surrounded by solvent molecules; such a program seems however beyond the capabilities of even the fastest computers available at present. We shall therefore considerably simplify the problem, (a) by replacing the true dynamical motion by Brownian Dynamics, and (b) by using a lattice model for describing the macromolecule.

articleTitle: Influence of measurement inaccuracy on the charge distribution evaluated with the thermal-pulse technique
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Several papers<sup>1–4</sup> have reported on the measurement of the mean depth of charge distributions in dielectrics. Recent publications by Collins,<sup>5,6</sup> Laurenceau et al.,<sup>7,8</sup> Sessler et al.<sup>9</sup> and Andress et al.<sup>10</sup> are directed towards the determination of the detailed spatial charge distributions. In a very recent letter DeReggi et al.<sup>11</sup> showed that the thermal-pulse technique only delivers the first 10–15 Fourier coefficients of the charge distribution.

articleTitle: Currents from squid giant axons clamped with their action potentials
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: The Hodgkin-Huxley equations<sup>1</sup> have been used extensively to derive currents through membranes of squid giant axon. The Hodgkin-Huxley model postulates two independent ensembles of molecular channels which become accessible to K<sup>+</sup> and Na<sup>+</sup> ion currents respectively when they change from a closed to an open configuration. The membrane conductance is directly proportional to the number of “open” channels in each ensemble. With this arrangement, the current-voltage relationship is ohmic although the membrane conductance increases as the number of open channels increases. The rate constants for the closed-open kinetics are functions of the transmembrane potential.

articleTitle: Chemically stimulated current and ESR studies of charge storage
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: During the last few years, many powerful methods for studying the storage and polarization processes in dielectrics have been developed. They are essentially based on the analysis of the time or temperature dependence of the charge or polarization stored in the material. This has led to the knowledge of phenomenological parameters (trap depths, activation energies, carrier lifetimes, etc.) which are of great practical value but which only give informations on a macroscopic scale (except in some ideal crystalline structures).

articleTitle: Dielectric properties of protein-methylglyoxal complexes
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Pure proteins are insulators at normal temperatures because the energy gap between the valence and conduction bands is at least 4 eV and can be as large as 11.6 eV.<sup>1</sup> Apart from electrode injection effects, electronic conduction can therefore only occur as the result of charge-transfer interactions where electrons are either removed from the valence band or injected into the conduction band. Previous investigations have shown that when white proteins (such as bovine serum albumin, casein, collagen, or lysozyme) are complexed with methylglyoxal they assume a stable brown colour, and as a result of an assumed charge-transfer interaction they exhibit an enhanced d.c. electronic conductivity<sup>2</sup> and a pronounced dielectric dispersion at subHertz frequencies.<sup>3,4</sup> These studies have been continued in our laboratory and some of this extended work is described here. The methods of chemical preparation of the protein samples and the various electronic and dielectric measurement techniques used, have been described in detail in references given in the earlier reports.<sup>2,3,4</sup>

articleTitle: The clinical applications of ‘in-vivo’ measurements of dielectric properties of human tissue
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Schwan<sup>1</sup> in his review of the electrical properties of tissue and cell suspensions, noted the wide frequency spectrum over which dispersion regions can be expected. The values of the dielectric constant at low frequencies were likely to be very high. Fricke and Morse<sup>2</sup> found that the capacitance of excised breast tumour tissue was very different from that of excised normal breast tissue. These two observations have provided the rationale for the production of a piece of equipment to make rapid measurements of dielectric properties over a wide frequency spectrum and to investigate its possible clinical value in the field of breast cancer. There has been much work on various forms of in-vivo dielectric measurement, although they have usually been made in terms of electrical impendance, this work has been reviewed by Nyboer<sup>3</sup> and by Markovich.<sup>4</sup>

articleTitle: One-carrier thermally stimulated currents and space-charge-limited currents in naphthalene crystals
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: It is well known that the measurement of space-charge-limited currents in solids is a powerful tool for detecting low density carriers traps. But measurement of thermally stimulated currents is also a good method for determining trapping parameters in dielectric materials. Each method has specific limitations, so it is interesting to carry out both techniques. We have used both SCLC and TSC to study naphthalene single crystals.

articleTitle: X-ray destruction of impurity-vacancy dipoles in KCl:Eu2+
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: X-irradiation of KCl:Eu<sup>2+</sup> at room temperature destroyed impurity-vacancy (I-V) dipoles, converted the doubly-valent impurity ion to a singly-valent state, and created defect centers, e.g. F-centers and a 220 nm optical absorption band. Eu<sup>+</sup> produced by the irradiation was observed to grow in proportion to the destruction of The 220 nm band was also observed to grow approximately in proportion to the height of the F-band, in agreement with previous workers. The number of dipoles destroyed was equal to or exceeded the sum of the number of converted ions and the number of F-centers produced. To explain these results it is proposed that X-rays increase the rate of aggregation of dipoles, and that it is the cation vacancies bound in I-V dipoles that are converted to anion vacancies which later form F-centers.

articleTitle: Thermally stimulated current in elongated polyethylene by gamma radiation
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Three thermally stimulated current peaks were found at 35, 45 and 60°C in low density polyethylene film above room temperature, and the experiment on elongated samples showed that the second peak at 45°C was increased for draw ratios up to 200% and decreased for draw ratio over 200%. The temperatures of the three peaks and the heights at 35°C and 60°C were not affected by elongation. One of the possibilities of the increase and decrease of the height of peaks at 45°C may be ascribed to disruption of crystalline lamellae and the melt recrystallization due to elongation as indicated by X-ray long spacing measurements.

articleTitle: Relation between dielectric breakdown and morphological structure in polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: The effect of structural changes on the electrical impulse breakdown strength resulting from uni-axial drawing in low density polyethylene was previously reported at this Conference.<sup>1</sup> Increased impulse breakdown strength for increased draw ratio in film drawn at room temperature seemed to correlate with increasing the c-axis orientation function F<inf>c</inf> and decreasing the a-axis orientation function F<inf>a</inf> of crystalline lamellae. The breakdown strength in films drawn at 120°C on the other hand, was almost constant with drawing up to 90% draw ratio and increased monotonically thereafter. This characteristic can be related to the nearly constant F<inf>c</inf> up to 90% draw ratio and an increasing F<inf>c</inf> afterward.

articleTitle: Schottky polarization of gamma-irradiated teflon — A possible pitfall for TSC measurements
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Several authors<sup>1,2</sup> have measured thermally stimulated currents (TSC) by applying an external voltage to electroded insulating films previously irradiated with gamma rays. During such measurements with normally non-polar thin Teflon FEP and PTFE foils we have found a similar polarization effect. A reverse current is observed if a poled and heated sample is temporarily short-circuited; an “overshoot” of the current is observed if after short-circuiting the external bias is applied again. The time constant of the effect places it well beyond that of the capacitive currents that are observed under the same conditions.

articleTitle: Accelerated life testing of solid dielectric cables
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: The achievement of an accelerated laboratory test capable of predicting the useful service life of products has been an elusive goal for most manufactures. This state of affairs applies to solid dielectric cables functioning in complex environments. The community of interests concerned with electrical power transmission and distribution has long been aware of the lack of a suitable test. It has devised a wide assortment of procedures for evaluating the performance of cable designs and materials, but they do not provide accurate validatable estimates of service life under normal operating conditions. In common with most tests that are loosely labeled “accelerated” they are upon close examination useful mostly for quality control and comparative purposes.

articleTitle: Impulse breakdown in PMMA under megavolt, nanosecond excitation
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Factors that affect the breakdown strength of a solid dielectric include the electrode geometry, specimen thickness, specimen homogeneity, and the nature of the applied electrical excitation. In some applications, thick solid dielectrics are subjected to extremely high fields for periods of nanoseconds. The integrity of such systems cannot be extrapolated from the behavior of thinner dielectrics or from dielectrics subjected to longer pulses. Moreover, experiments on thick specimens in the nanosecond time regime have a particular interest because they can yield information on the mechanism of breakdown. The goal of the present work is to obtain this information on the mechanism of breakdown in solids. Single impulse excitation is employed, each impulse having an amplitude in the mega-volt range, large enough to highly overvolt relatively thick specimens while using a uniform field geometry. The damage morphology is examined.

articleTitle: On the mechanism of discharge propagation at the surface of an electrolyte
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Flashover of high voltage polluted insulators occurs in two successive phases: 1 — appearance of a discharge at the surface of the wet insulator; 2 — elongation to flashover if electrical conditions are favorable. The triggering phenomenon for the first phase has long been identified as being dry band formation.<sup>1</sup>

articleTitle: Electrical behavior of crosslinked dielectric materials at elevated temperatures
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: An extensive study has been carried out into the electrical behavior of crosslinkable dielectric materials at elevated temperatures under a reserach contract from the Electric Power Research Institute. This work is part of a program to establish emergency operating guidelines for extruded solid dielectric power cables. Materials studied include XLPE, filled XLPE and EPR compounds. The A. C. and impulse breakdown strengths, A. C. loss and dielectric constant, d.c. resistivity and corona degradation, were investigated for a range, of temperatures between 25°C and 170°C. The effect of the degree of crosslinking in XLPE was investigated and measurements were performed on laboratory molded specimens as well as specimen cut from full size extruded power cables. The results will be discussed in the framework of current models of conduction and breakdown in high polymers. The overall electrical performance of crosslinked dielectric materials at elevated temperature will be discussed as regards to their use in solid dielectric power cables.

articleTitle: Non-linear dielectric properties of biological materials
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: It is proposed to report on the progress made since my 1974 Whitehead Memorial Lecture on the extraordinary dielectric properties of biological materials. It will be remembered that from very general considerations it can be concluded that large polarizable molecules are expected to possess metastable states with very high electric dipole moment. The conditions to which this transition is subjected will be presented. Already in 1972 it had been suggested that this property might be relevant for an understanding of the gating mechanism in nerve membranes. Some further progress in this direction has been made.

articleTitle: Charging of polymers by high electric fields
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Several polar and non-polar polymers, including polyvinylidene fluoride, polyethylene and polytetra-fluoroethylene were charged by evaporating various metal electrodes onto films of the materials and applying electric fields of the order of 1 MV/cm at various temperatures and times. The charged films were then analyzed by observing the charge transient which results during thermal equilibration following the heating of the electrodes with short (∼1 μsec) pulses of light (thermal pulse measurement of charge distribution due to R. E. Collins). The observed transients are discussed in terms of the charge distributions in the polymers and the relationship between these distributions and the sample history. The usefulness of considering the polymers as having a work function and possible implications of high-field charging on the breakdown strength of solid polymers will be discussed.

articleTitle: Computer simulation of charge dynamics in electron-irradiated polymer foils
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Electron irradiation in a good dielectric, such as a Teflon polymer, both deposits electrons in the material and, simultaneously, induces significant conductivity. Considerable work has been done to understand the resulting transient (e.g. see refs. 1–7) and steady-state charge behavior (e.g. see refs. 8 and 9). Most theoretical studies have assumed uniform, time-indëpendent, induced conductivity and electron-beam current (implying a single electron range) in the irradiated region. Two recent exceptions are the numerical studies of Matsuoka et al.,<sup>10</sup> Beers<sup>11</sup> and, Gross and Leal Fereira<sup>12</sup> who have relaxed the single electron-range assumption for time-independent parameters. Also, with the exception of Gross and Oliveira<sup>7,8</sup> and a later paper by Aris, Davies and Lewis,<sup>9</sup> previous work has treated linearized transport equations only.

articleTitle: An electrical barrier model for flicker noise in biological membranes
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Biological membranes, having a thickness of approximately 30A and consisting of more or less ordered arrays of lipid and protein molecules form an essential part of all living cells. The lipid molecules in particular with polar head groups and hydrocarbon tails are oriented to form bilayers in which the hydophilic head groups are in contact with aqueous electrolyte phases on either side (Fig. 1). In spite of the presence of the electrolyte and the fact that the system is water permeable, these bilayers are strongly insulating in biological terms and regularly sustain fields of ∼10<sup>7</sup> Vm<sup>−1</sup>. The parallel with solid state insulating films such as oxide layers is apparent and thus such bilayers are of interest not only to biologists but also to physicists, especially as stable artificial bilayers — to so-called black lipid membranes — may be produced to have many of the electrical properties of the natural ones.<sup>2</sup> Although membranes are permeable to alkali ions such as K<sup>+</sup> and Na<sup>+</sup>, which pass from one aqueous phase to the other, the process is energetically discouraged not only because of the low permittivity of the hydrocarbon tails of the lipids but also because their semi-crystalline ordered structure will require deformation to permit ion passage.

articleTitle: Thermally stimulated current measurements on PTFE electrets
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Important in any practical use of electrets is the charge retention time and therefore device lifetime. Since charge retention times are on the order of years for many electret materials, accelerated tests are used where the driving force is increased temperature. In this preliminary study, three tests were used all using elevated temperatures: short-circuit thermally stimulated current measurements (short-circuit TSCs), open-circuit thermally stimulated current measurements (open-circuit TSCs), and isothermal charge decay measurements. These three techniques offer different perspectives of studying charge movement.

articleTitle: Time domain spectroscopy and its value in measuring the permittivity of biological specimens
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Molecules of interest to the biophysicist have been studied with dielectric techniques for many years. However, the traditional approach has been to dissolve the molecule in an aqueous solution and then to measure its dielectric properties in the frequency domain. This involves measuring the complex permittivity Ε = E' − CE″ at many individual frequency points (ideally greater than 30) over a wide frequency range (from the kHz into the GHz region). Such techniques suffer from the following problems.

articleTitle: The dielectric and thermal behavior of solid solutions of thiacyclohexane and tetrahydropyran
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Thiacyclohexane has been extensively investigated by a number of authors<sup>1–3</sup> and has been found to exist in three crystal forms. Kondo and Matsumoto<sup>3</sup> refer to these forms as I, II and III where I refers to the high temperature phase and III to the low temperature phase. This notation will be used throughout this paper. The high temperature form (I) is found to be plastic in nature;<sup>4</sup> that is to say, it exhibits a low entropy of fusion and plastic flow under pressure. This behaviour is due to the high degree of orientational freedom possessed by the molecules as a result of their ability to rotate in the solid state. The crystal has been found to be a face-centered cubic lattice.<sup>2</sup>

articleTitle: Bioelectrets
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: The electret state has been reported now for many important biological molecules.<sup>1</sup> Most biopolymers<sup>2</sup> such as proteins, polysaccharides and polynucleotides were found to present charge and polarization storage via the electret state. The term bioelectret has been proposed<sup>1</sup> to indicate the possible biological and biophysical applications of the concept. Bioelectrets have been proposed to play a role in membranes,<sup>3</sup> enzymes<sup>4</sup>'<sup>5</sup> and other biological systems. The sources for polarization storage in a bioelectret such as a biopolymer may have various origins: dipolar residues, ions related to the polyelectrolyte behaviour of the biopolymers, and bound-water. Using thermally stimulated depolarization (TSD), isothermal polarization (IP) and thermally stimulated pressure (TSP) measurements to monitor the dehydration of the bioelectret it has been possible to study the influence of bound water in systems such as lysozyme.<sup>6</sup>

articleTitle: Dielectric loss measurements of polymers in the frequency range 0.1 to 30 MHz under very high hydrostatic pressure (1 to 1500 bar)
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: The dielectric loss measurements of submarine telecommunication cables can be determined under use conditions with our experimental apparatus. The principle of measurement is based on the air substitution technique, using a Hewlett Packard 4342 Q meter and a General Radio 1690 A dielectric sample holder. The later is located within a hydrostatic pressure bomb. The pressure transmitting fluid is gaseous argon or nitrogen. Measurements may be made over the temperature range −5°C to +50°C. The resolution in loss angle measurement is approximately ±2 μ radian at 30 MHz. All the displacements of the upper electrode of the sample holder operated during measurement at atmospheric pressure are controlled by an appropriate motors driving system. The results obtained with the polyethylene used as submarine telecommunication cable insulation showed a significant variation of its loss angle with pressure.

articleTitle: On the calculation of piezoelectricity and pyroelectricity in polyvinylidene fluoride
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Piezoelectric and pyroelectric properties of poly-vinylidene fluoride (PVDF) and related semicrystalline polymers are receiving increasing attention as these polymers find use in transducer applications. This paper considers some of the microscopic features of PVDF and calculates the electrical response of a model based on these features.

articleTitle: Electronic excitations and radiation damage in polymers
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Electron energy loss spectroscopy is an attractive technique for measuring the spectrum of electronic excitations in polymers. Spectra can be recorded over the entire energy range of valence and core electronic excitations from 1 to 400 eV with a resolution of 0.1 eV. The experiments reported here measured energy loss spectra of an 80 keV electron beam with an intensity of 6.5 × 10<sup>−7</sup> amp/cm<sup>2</sup> transmitted through thin films (−1000 Å) of polystyrene (PS), poly (2-vinylpyridine) (PVP), polyethylene (PE) and polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA), prepared by standard solvent casting techniques. The special purpose high resolution energy loss spectrometer, similar in design to a new 300 keV instrument,<sup>1</sup> is capable of obtaining spectra before significant radiation damage effects are observed.

articleTitle: Effect on molecular weight distributions of polyethylene after ion implantation
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Discharges in dielectric materials are known to cause some, at least, of the failures observed during service. A major factor limiting the life of polyethylene cables, for example, is believed to be progressive deterioration due to discharges in gas-filled cavities. The characteristics of their development has been studied.<sup>1–3</sup>

articleTitle: Kerr type electro-optical effects in solid dielectrics
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Kerr type<sup>1,2</sup> electro-optical effects have been detected and measured over a range of temperatures in polymethyl-methacrylate (PMMA). The observed birefringence is very much lower than in nitrobenzene, for example. It nonetheless appears possible that the Kerr effect in solid dielectrics may be used to map electric field intensities around electrodes, voids or inclusions in a manner similar to that in liquid Kerr cells.<sup>3–5</sup>

articleTitle: X-ray induced TSC and RIC in polyvinylidene fluoride
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1978
abstract: Carrier trapping phenomena in polymers greatly influence not only their electric conduction process but, through the introduction of space charge, also influence the dielectric breakdown phenomena. Thermally stimulated current (TSC) and thermoluminescence (TL) from polymers have been widely investigated to clarify the nature of carrier traps. However, the low concentration of carriers in polymeric insulators often makes it difficult to analyze their nature. To eliminate this problem, radiation induced phenomena have been intensively investigated. Radiation induced TSC and TL experiments have provided a great deal of information about the nature of carrier traps in polymers and their relation to morphology and molecular motions has been pointed out.
